sections.heading: What is Ultrasonic Testing (UT)?
body: At OAGITECH Oil & Gas Inspection Technology, Ultrasonic Testing (UT), sometimes referred to as a sonic test, operates by transmitting high-frequency sound waves into a material to evaluate its internal structure. This non-destructive inspection method helps detect hidden flaws without damaging the tested component.

When the sound waves travel through the material and encounter discontinuities such as cracks, voids, or material boundaries, the waves are reflected back to the inspection probe. By analyzing the strength and timing of these reflected signals, inspectors can accurately determine the presence, size, and location of potential defects.

sections.heading: How Ultrasonic Inspection Works
body: Ultrasonic inspection is a non-destructive testing technique that uses high-frequency sound waves to identify internal defects and evaluate material integrity without causing any damage.
The inspection process generally involves the following steps:
A transducer transmits high-frequency sound waves into the tested material or component.
When the waves encounter discontinuities such as cracks or thickness changes, they are reflected back to the probe.
These reflected signals are displayed on a monitoring screen, allowing inspectors to analyze the presence, size, and location of potential defects.

At OAGITECH Oil & Gas Inspection Technology, ultrasonic testing is widely used to obtain accurate and reliable inspection results for both surface and subsurface evaluations, ensuring the quality and structural reliability of critical components and welded structures.

Radiographic Testing (RT) is a non-destructive testing technique that uses X-rays or gamma radiation to produce images of the internal structure of materials and components. This method allows inspectors to detect hidden defects without damaging the tested object.
Applications of Radiographic Testing

sections.heading: Radiographic Testing Techniques
body: Film Radiography vs. Digital Radiography
At OAGITECH, we provide both film radiography and digital radiography solutions to meet different inspection and documentation requirements.

Film Radiography This traditional inspection method produces a physical radiographic film that serves as a permanent record of the inspection. It is commonly used when long-term archival documentation and verification are required.

Digital Radiography Digital radiography allows for faster image processing, improved data storage, and easier image analysis. This modern approach is particularly effective for projects requiring high inspection volumes, rapid reporting, and remote collaboration.

Real-Time Radiography (RTR) for Immediate Image Analysis Real-Time Radiography (RTR) enables inspectors to observe X-ray images instantly as they are captured. This capability allows for immediate evaluation and quicker identification of potential defects during the inspection process

sections.heading: Gamma Ray Testing vs. X-Ray Testing

items.title: Gamma Ray Testing: This technique is ideal for the inspection of dense materials or where locations have limited access. It uses radioactive isotopes and is often used in confined or remote settings.

sections.heading: What is Magnetic Particle Testing?
body: Magnetic Particle Testing (MPT) is a non-destructive testing method used to identify surface and near-surface defects in ferromagnetic materials. The process involves magnetizing the component and applying fine magnetic particles to the surface. If a crack or discontinuity is present, it disturbs the magnetic field, causing the particles to accumulate at the defect location and form a visible indication.

items.title: Inspection under proper lighting
items.text: Observing the test surface under appropriate lighting conditions to detect visible indications of defects.

items.title: Demagnetization and cleaning
items.text: Removing residual magnetism and cleaning the component after the inspection is complete.

subs.heading: Overview of Dye Penetrant Testing (PT) in NDT

subs.heading: How Liquid Penetrant Testing Works
body: Liquid penetrant testing involves applying a visible or fluorescent dye to a clean and dry surface. The penetrant seeps into any surface defects through capillary action, making otherwise invisible flaws detectable.

After allowing sufficient dwell time, excess penetrant is carefully removed, and a developer is applied. The developer draws out the trapped penetrant from defects, creating clear and visible indications that can be easily inspected and evaluated

Conventional NDT methods (i.e. manual UT or MPI) rely heavily on operator interpretation and surface-level defects. Advanced techniques use digital tools, phased arrays, sensors and automation to:

items.title: Detect flaws deep within complex geometrics
Map corrosion or thickness loss over large surface areas
Produce permanent digital records for traceability
Enable real-time data visuals and remove assessment

subs.heading: Advanced Ultrasonic Testing (AUT)
body: AUT uses automated probes and scanners to deliver consistent and detailed inspection data across welds, pipe walls, and structural components.

subs.heading: Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing (PAUT)
body: Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing (PAUT) offers multi-angle scans of welds and components. This is ideal for thick sections, curved surfaces and time-sensitive inspections.

subs.heading: Time-of-Flight Diffraction (TOFD)
body: TOFD uses sound wave timing to measure crack depth and growth. This is particularly effective in pressure vessel inspection and long seam welds.

subs.heading: Acoustic Emission Testing for Structural Integrity
body: Acoustic Emission Testing detects active flaws as they occur. This makes it ideal for monitoring structural components under stress.

subs.heading: Vacuum Box Testing for Leak Detection
body: Vacuum box testing is a quick and effective way to detect leaks in weld seams and seams on tanks, vessels, and pipelines.

subs.heading: Holiday Testing for Coating Defects
body: Holiday testing detects pinholes or thin areas in protective coatings, supporting corrosion protection in offshore and subsea assets.

subs.heading: Vibration Analysis of Rotating Equipment
body: Vibration analysis helps to identify imbalances, misalignment or early bearing failure in motors, turbines and compressors.

subs.heading: Total Focusing Method (TFM)
body: The Total Focusing Method (TFM) is an advanced evolution of Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing (PAUT), offering full matrix capture (FMC) data acquisition and reconstruction. Unlike conventional PAUT, which relies on pre-set angles and beam steering, TFM digitally focuses at every pixel in the region of interest, producing superior image resolution and flaw characterization.

subs.heading: Thermal and Infrared-Based Testing
body: We use infrared thermograph to assess electrical panels, insulation systems and rotating equipment for heat anomalies and internal defects.

subs.heading: Magnetic Flux Leakage (MFL)
body: Magnetic Flux Leakage (MFL) is widely used for detecting corrosion and pitting on tank floors by measuring disturbances in a magnetized steel plate. The technique provides rapid scanning and high sensitivity to both surface and near-surface defects. It enables efficient mapping of large floor areas, helping prioritize repairs and extend tank service life. MFL can also be applied through coatings and linings, minimizing surface preparation requirements during inspection.
